papers.title: Creative Demands and Practical Limitations of Controllable Music Generation from the Human Perception Perspective
papers.abstract: Controllable music generation aims to allow creators to guide AI in music creation through intuitive means, but the existing systems are still far from achieving this goal. From the perspective of human perception, this study combines computer music education and practical experience to explore the actual demands of creators for a generation system in terms of timbre control, rhythm arrangement, emotional expression, and editability of results. The study found that current controllable music generation has three deficiencies: First, there is a semantic mismatch between the system's parameter settings and the auditory perception of creators, and the adjustable dimensions are difficult to align with intuitive judgments in music creation; Second, the response of the generation model to control instructions lacks stability and precision, and there are frequent deviations between the creative concept and the final output; Third, the existing tools do not support an iterative workflow of repeated listening and local modification in music production, making it difficult to further edit and refine the generated results. The above problems show that, in order to serve the creative needs of people in their work, controllable music generation should be based on their perception habits and working methods rather than technical performance optimisation.

papers.title: Clinical Praat Parameters and Cepstral Representations for Speaker-Independent Voice Pathology Detection: The Influence of Age and Dysphonia Severity.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES To determine whether clinically validated Praat parameters discriminate pathological from healthy voice under speaker-independent evaluation of the complete Saarbrücken Voice Database corpus of sustained vowels, how their performance compares with a high-dimensional cepstral representation and a speech foundation model trained through self-supervision, and how discrimination depends on dysphonia severity and on the age difference between groups. STUDY DESIGN Retrospective analysis of a publicly available voice database. The machine learning task was formulated as binary classification: healthy versus pathological voice. METHODS All 15,442 sustained vowel recordings from 1288 sessions of 1180 speakers (age 27.9 ± 11.7 years in healthy and 50.7 ± 15.4 years in pathological speakers) were analyzed. A total of 78 features were extracted: 14 clinical parameters via Praat and 64 cepstral, spectral, and energy descriptors via librosa. Group differences were tested at the session level with Mann-Whitney U, quantified by rank-biserial correlation, and corrected by Holm-Bonferroni. Six classifiers were compared using nested cross-validation with five folds grouped by speaker. The severity of acoustic alteration was estimated with the Acoustic Voice Quality Index (AVQI), which does not replace perceptual evaluation, and age was controlled by matching patients to controls on age and sex and by reweighting the training data. RESULTS Nine of 11 parameters reached medium effect size, led by jitter PPQ5 (r = -0.414) and CPPS (r = +0.382). Sixty percent of pathological sessions had acoustic voice quality within the healthy range. The SVM (0.775 ± 0.019) and XGBoost (0.770 ± 0.013) reached the highest recording-level AUC; adapted wav2vec 2.0 reached 0.726 ± 0.015. The 14 Praat parameters and the 52 cepstral coefficients performed similarly (AUC difference +0.014, 95% CI -0.002 to +0.030); neither equivalence nor superiority was demonstrated. With age controlled, XGBoost reached a session-level AUC of 0.721 (95% CI 0.669 to 0.769). Discrimination increased progressively across strata of acoustic alteration defined by the AVQI: 0.60 within the healthy range and 0.89 to 0.99 above it. Jitter, shimmer, and CPPS kept their effect sizes after age matching, whereas f0 variability did not. CONCLUSIONS Acoustic analysis of sustained vowels identifies dysphonia with measurable acoustic alteration but not acoustically mild disorders, and 14 interpretable parameters performed similarly to a cepstral representation nearly four times larger. Discrimination reported on the SVD should be interpreted in the light of the age difference between groups and the severity composition of the sample.

# StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

```bibtex
            on Edge GPUs in Rust},

}
```

# ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo (4B) for music-gen (ONNX)

This is the ACE-Step 1.5 **XL turbo** model (the 4B DiT: 8 steps, no CFG) converted to ONNX: its
condition encoder (FP32) and its DiT (BF16 inside, with FP32 inputs and output). It's made for
music-gen, a local ACE-Step 1.5 text-to-music runner on ONNX Runtime and CUDA. A whole pipeline
also needs:
- `music-gen-qwen3-embedding-0.6b-onnx`, the caption and lyric encoders;
- `music-gen-ace-step-v15-vae-onnx`, the VAE and silence latent.

The source is `ACE-Step/acestep-v15-xl-turbo` at revision
`d4a0b288b83ebb7e25a8c0b32c573c22e134e8ee`, run with the modeling code shipped beside it.

## Files

**`condition_xl_turbo.onnx`** (+ `.data`, 2.4 GB, FP32): XL's condition encoder, with the same
inputs, outputs and limits as the 2B's (see `music-gen-ace-step-v15-turbo-onnx`). XL's timbre
encoder prepends a CLS token; that's inside the graph.

**`dit_xl_turbo.onnx`** (+ `.data`, 8.3 GB, BF16 inside):
- **Inputs:** `hidden_states` [1, T, 64], `timestep` [1], `encoder_hidden_states` [1, E, 2048],
  `context_latents` [1, T, 128].
- **Output:** `velocity` [1, T, 64].
- **Limits:** T even, 16–15000; E 2–4096.
- **Fits on a 24 GB GPU** up to about 7 minutes (T 10500); see Memory.

`SHA256SUMS` lists every file's sha256. Sampling is the same as the 2B turbo's: the shift-3 turbo
schedule, Euler steps, and x0 at the last step.

## Precision

- **Why not FP16:** XL overflows in FP16. Its residual stream passes 65504 in the first layer, in
  PyTorch too.
- **Why not FP32:** about 16 GB of weights would leave no room for a long piece's activations.
- **So BF16, as upstream runs it on CUDA, with two exceptions:**
  - **The attention scores and softmax run in FP32.** Split into ONNX ops, BF16 scores made long
    sequences 2–3 times less accurate than upstream; upstream's fused kernel keeps them in FP32
    inside.
  - **The two patch convolutions (`proj_in`, `proj_out`) run in FP32,** because ONNX's `Conv` takes
    no BF16 at opset 18.

## Accuracy

The FP32 condition encoder against PyTorch FP32: 9.7e-9 on unpadded inputs, 3.9–4.1e-7 with
padding.

The BF16 DiT against PyTorch **FP32**, relative RMS error. Upstream's own BF16 is the yardstick,
and our graph has to stay within 1.5 times it to pass:

| Case | This graph | Upstream's BF16 |
|---|---|---|
| T=200, E=86 | 4.5e-2 | 4.4e-2 |
| T=750, E=86 | 4.9e-2 | 4.5e-2 |
| T=750, E=300 | 6.4e-2 | 6.6e-2 |
| T=1500, E=40 | 4.6e-2 | 4.1e-2 |

## Memory and speed (RTX 3090, 24 GB)

| Length | Time | Peak |
|---|---|---|
| 30 s | 8–9 s, loading included | 9.5–11.6 GB |
| 3 min | 13.5 s | 15.3 GB |
| 5 min | 20.5 s | 22.9 GB |
| 7 min | 29.5 s | 20.8 GB |
| 8 min | 33.5 s | 24.1 GB (at the limit) |
| 9 min | fails | |

The FP32 attention scores grow as 32 heads × T²/4. For pieces longer than 7 minutes on a 24 GB GPU,
use the 2B turbo, which goes to 10.

## How it was made

The scripts are included in `export/`:
- `condition.py` is the same as for the 2B.
- `dit.py` is run with `bf16`. It loads the checkpoint in BF16, registers an attention function
  with FP32 scores and softmax, and wraps the two convolutions in FP32. It exports with
  `torch.onnx.export(dynamo=True)` at opset 18 and checks the result against PyTorch FP32 and BF16,
  each stage in its own process.

Packages: torch 2.10.0+cu128, transformers 4.57.6, accelerate 1.13.0, onnx 1.23.2,
onnxscript 0.7.2, onnxruntime-gpu 1.24.4.

## Licence and changes

MIT (`LICENSE`), as the original, copyright (c) 2026 ACEStep. **Changed:** converted from
safetensors to ONNX; the condition encoder and DiT were split out of the model and wrapped as
described above; the DiT's weights were cast to BF16, with attention scores and the two
convolutions in FP32. Nothing was retrained or quantised further.

```bibtex
    howpublished={\url{https://github.com/ace-step/ACE-Step-1.5}},
    year={2026},
    note={GitHub repository}
}
```

# ACE-Step 1.5 turbo (2B) for music-gen (ONNX, FP32)

This is the ACE-Step 1.5 **turbo** model (the 2B DiT: 8 steps, no CFG) converted to ONNX: its
condition encoder and its DiT. It's made for music-gen, a local ACE-Step 1.5 text-to-music runner
on ONNX Runtime and CUDA. A whole pipeline also needs:
- `music-gen-qwen3-embedding-0.6b-onnx`, the caption and lyric encoders;
- `music-gen-ace-step-v15-vae-onnx`, the VAE and silence latent.

The source is `ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5` at revision `19671f406d603126926c1b7e2adc169acbcade22`,
`acestep-v15-turbo/` (`model.safetensors` sha256 `3f6e0797…6e422d7`), run with the modeling code
shipped beside it.

> Why not an existing ONNX export? The community export `shreyask/ACE-Step-v1.5-ONNX` has a DiT
> whose weights aren't this checkpoint's: 81 of its 110 named weights differ, so it makes noise from
> any input. Its condition encoder's lyric part is also wrong unless the lyrics are padded to 2048
> tokens. These graphs were exported from the checkpoint itself and checked against it.

## Files

**`condition_turbo.onnx`** (+ `.data`, 2.4 GB): ACE-Step's condition encoder (text projector, lyric
encoder, timbre encoder, packing), plus `prepare_condition`'s
`src = where(is_covers > 0, hints, src_latents)` and `context = [src, chunk_masks]`.
- **Inputs:** `text_hidden_states` [1, ts, 1024], `text_attention_mask` [1, ts],
  `lyric_hidden_states` [1, ls, 1024], `lyric_attention_mask` [1, ls],
  `refer_audio_acoustic_hidden_states_packed` [1, rl, 64], `refer_audio_order_mask` int64 [1],
  `src_latents` [1, t, 64], `chunk_masks` [1, t, 64], `is_covers` [1],
  `precomputed_lm_hints_25hz` [1, t, 64].
- **Outputs:** `encoder_hidden_states` [1, ts+ls+1, 2048], `encoder_attention_mask` [1, ts+ls+1],
  `context_latents` [1, t, 128].
- **Limits:** one batch item and one reference clip (the timbre unpacking for that case);
  ts 2–512, ls 2–4096, rl 2–15000, t 2–15000.

**`dit_turbo.onnx`** (+ `.data`, 6.3 GB): the DiT, called as ACE-Step's sampler calls it
(`timestep_r = timestep`, no cache).
- **Inputs:** `hidden_states` [1, T, 64], `timestep` [1], `encoder_hidden_states` [1, E, 2048],
  `context_latents` [1, T, 128].
- **Output:** `velocity` [1, T, 64].
- **Limits:** T even, 16–15000 (up to 10 minutes at 25 frames a second); E 2–4096.

All tensors are float32 except where marked. `SHA256SUMS` lists every file's sha256.

**Sampling,** as ACE-Step's turbo does it:
- Start from Gaussian noise [1, T, 64].
- Use the shift-3 schedule `[1.0, 0.95455, 0.9, 0.83333, 0.75, 0.64286, 0.5, 0.3]`.
- Each step does `x -= v · (t_k − t_{k+1})`; the last step does `x0 = x − v · t`.
- Decode x0 with the VAE.

For text-to-music, `src_latents` is the silence latent tiled to T, `chunk_masks` is all ones and
`is_covers` is 0. For repainting a span, `src_latents` is the existing latent with the span set to
silence and `chunk_masks` is 1 over the span.

## How it was made

The scripts are included in `export/`:
- `condition.py` exports with `torch.onnx.export(dynamo=True)` at opset 18. Two of upstream's
  functions are replaced during the export only, each with an exact equivalent: the stable argsort
  in `pack_sequences` (for 0/1 masks, sorting a unique key gives the same order, and ONNX has no
  stable sort) and the timbre unpacking (its one-batch case).
- `dit.py` runs each stage (PyTorch's reference answers, the export, the check) in its own process.

Packages: torch 2.10.0+cu128, transformers 4.57.6, onnx 1.23.2, onnxscript 0.7.2,
onnxruntime-gpu 1.24.4.

## Accuracy

Against upstream's PyTorch FP32 on CUDA, with TF32 off, as relative RMS error:

| Graph | Results |
|---|---|
| `condition_turbo` | 7e-9 to 9e-9 on unpadded inputs; up to 4.0e-7 with padded captions and lyrics (text 256 / lyrics 2048 with masks; text 30 / lyrics 600 at 1501 frames) |
| `dit_turbo` | 1.5e-5 at T=200, 4.0e-6 at 750, 5.0e-6 at 750 with 300 condition tokens, 8.3e-6 at 1500 |
| All 8 steps, against upstream's own sampler on the same noise | 4.8e-6 at 750 frames (30 s); 7.9e-5 at 15000 frames (10 min) |

On an RTX 3090 (24 GB): a 3-minute piece takes about 10 s with a 10.3 GB peak; a 10-minute piece
takes 29 s with a 16.7–19.8 GB peak.

## Licence and changes

MIT (`LICENSE`), as the original, copyright (c) 2026 ACEStep. **Changed:** converted from
safetensors to ONNX; the condition encoder and DiT were split out of the model and wrapped as
described above. Nothing was retrained or quantised.

Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E（研究预览）

Sophon-Realtime v1 系列的端到端版：听和说用同一种向量语言
AI降临派（Adventists AI）· Apache-2.0

GitHub · Hugging Face · 魔搭 · English

> **研究预览。** 生产使用请选 [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag)（表现力最强，单卡）或 [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash)（最快、并发最高，单卡）。三个版本是同一个大脑，只有出声方式不同。 ## 这是什么 E2E 版不用单独的语音模型。32B 模型在听你说话时，内部会形成一串连续向量，里面既有说了什么，也有怎么说的（语调、轻重、情绪）。E2E 的说话头直接用这门「向量语言」写出回复，再由解码器还原成声音，所以模型听得懂的语气，它也能说出来。 ## 在 v1 系列里的位置 Sophon-Realtime v1 有三个版本，同一个大脑（VoiceBench 82.8、Big Bench Audio 81.8%，两项开源全双工第一；副语言理解综合第一），区别只在回复怎么变成声音： | | [Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag)（推荐） | [Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | **E2E（本仓库，研究预览）** | |---|---|---|---| | NVV-SuperBench（中 / 英） | **0.86 / 0.80** | 0.77 / 0.63 | 0.77 / 0.60 | | 单路首包 | 约 0.6 秒 | **0.31 秒** | 约 1 秒 | | 显卡 | 1 张 | 1 张 | 2 张 | E2E 适合研究端到端的语音表达；生产使用建议选 Tag 或 Flash。系列介绍和完整评测见 [v1 系列主页](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-v1)。 ## 本版更新（2026-11） - **解码器换代，4 步出声。** 每块音频的计算量与旧版相同。 - 同一说话头的回复上，与旧版解码器对比： | | 旧版（Sophon-Realtime-v1） | **本版** | |---|---|---| | 长回复错字率（150 条，中 / 英 / 日） | 1.78%（1.03 / 1.32 / 2.99） | **1.51%（0.97 / 0.71 / 2.86）** | | 未见说话人参考音色的相似度 | 0.33 | **0.52** | | 单路首包（发布包 bench，中位） | 0.57 s | **0.51 s** | - 旧版权重仍保留在 [Sophon-Realtime-v1](https://www.modelscope.cn/models/AdventistsAI/Sophon-Realtime-v1)。 ## 部署 两张 80 GB 显卡：思考器一张，说话引擎一张（说话引擎单卡建议 4–5 路并发）。需要 Linux、NVIDIA 驱动 580 及以上。 ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime cd sophon-realtime bash scripts/install.sh # 建两个虚拟环境，并从魔搭下载本模型 SOPHON_MODEL_DIR=$PWD/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E THINKER_GPU=0 TALKER_GPU=1 bash scripts/start.sh ``` 启动后打开 `http://<服务器>:8000/` 即可在网页里直接对话，也可以通过 WebSocket 接口（`/ws`）接入自己的客户端。说明见 GitHub 仓库的 [docs/deploy_CN.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/docs/deploy_CN.md)。 ## 文件 | 目录 | 内容 | |---|---| | `base/` | 32B 底座（思考器与说话头共用） | | `adapters/tag/` | 写回复的 LoRA | | `talker/` | 说话头 | | `e2/` | 解码器（4 步）与声码器 | | `voices/` | 默认音色 | ## 许可证 代码和权重都是 Apache-2.0。第三方组件保留各自的许可证，见 GitHub 仓库的 NOTICE。 ## 联系 商务合作：jiejin@adventists.ai --- # Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E (research preview) **The end-to-end build of the Sophon-Realtime v1 family: hearing and speaking share one vector language.** Adventists AI · Apache-2.0 > **Research preview.** For production, use [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) (most expressive, one GPU) or [Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) (fastest, most users per GPU, one GPU). All three share the same brain and differ only in how the reply becomes sound. ## What it is The E2E build speaks without a separate speech model. While the 32B model listens, it builds a stream of continuous vectors that carries both what was said and how (intonation, emphasis, emotion). The E2E talker writes replies directly in that vector language and a decoder turns it into sound, so the tone the model can hear is the tone it can speak. ## Where it fits in the v1 family Sophon-Realtime v1 has three builds that share one brain (VoiceBench 82.8 and Big Bench Audio 81.8%, #1 among open full-duplex models on both; #1 in paralinguistic understanding). They differ only in how the reply becomes sound: | | [Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) (recommended) | [Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash) | **E2E (this repository, research preview)** | |---|---|---|---| | NVV-SuperBench (zh / en) | **0.86 / 0.80** | 0.77 / 0.63 | 0.77 / 0.60 | | First audio, one user | ~0.6 s | **0.31 s** | ~1 s | | GPUs | 1 | 1 | 2 | E2E is for research on end-to-end expressive speech; for production, use Tag or Flash. Family overview and full benchmarks: [v1 family home page](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-v1). ## What's new (Nov 2026) - **New decoder, 4 steps.** Same compute per audio chunk as before. - Against the previous decoder, on replies from the same talker: | | previous (Sophon-Realtime-v1) | **this release** | |---|---|---| | Long replies, error rate (150 replies, zh / en / ja) | 1.78% (1.03 / 1.32 / 2.99) | **1.51% (0.97 / 0.71 / 2.86)** | | Voice similarity to an unseen reference speaker | 0.33 | **0.52** | | First audio, one user (release-package bench, median) | 0.57 s | **0.51 s** | - The previous weights stay in [Sophon-Realtime-v1](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-v1). ## Deployment Two 80 GB GPUs: one for the thinker, one for the speaking engine (4–5 concurrent conversations recommended per engine GPU). Linux with NVIDIA driver 580 or newer. ```bash git clone https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime cd sophon-realtime bash scripts/install.sh # two virtual environments + this model from ModelScope SOPHON_MODEL_DIR=$PWD/Sophon-Realtime-32B-E2E THINKER_GPU=0 TALKER_GPU=1 bash scripts/start.sh ``` Then open `http://:8000/` to talk in the browser, or connect your own client to the WebSocket API (`/ws`). See [docs/deploy.md](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime/blob/main/docs/deploy.md). ## Files | folder | contents | |---|---| | `base/` | 32B backbone (shared by the thinker and the talker) | | `adapters/tag/` | reply LoRA | | `talker/` | talker | | `e2/` | decoder (4 steps) and vocoder | | `voices/` | default voice | ## License Code and weights are released under Apache-2.0. Third-party components keep their own licences; see NOTICE in the GitHub repository. ## Contact Business enquiries: jiejin@adventists.ai

# DuplexJev-32B-Para (v1.5)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release notes: [hearing the whole clip (v1.5)](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-11-full-length.md) · [Japanese as a third language](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-japanese.md) · [weak languages](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md) · Research notes: [hearing stress](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-stress-understanding.md) · [keeping a speech-decision LLM able to talk](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-chat-replay.md)

🗣️ **Now with a voice:** DuplexJev-32B-Para is the ears of [Sophon-Realtime v1](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag), our open full-duplex voice model that hears your tone and speaks with one. Released: [Tag](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Tag) and [Flash](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/Sophon-Realtime-32B-Flash), one GPU each.

**The DuplexJev model that hears the most beyond the words.** On top of everything
[DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn) and
[DuplexJev-32B-Stress](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Stress) do (spoken QA, gender, emotion,
turn-taking, stress and pauses), it also hears **laughter, breathing, coughs and sighs**, notices **how** someone is
talking (whispering, shouting, very fast or slow), and can tell, roughly as a person would, **whether two clips are
the same speaker**. Mandarin and English. Since v1.1 it also **holds a normal conversation**, multi-turn included.
**v1.2** adds **accent judgments** (English accents and Mandarin dialect regions) and much sharper **end-of-turn
detection right after the user pauses**: on LiveKit's eot-bench it now beats Smart Turn v3.2 in English and Chinese.
**v1.3** hears **stress** much better: on the public StressTest benchmark it goes from 72 to **85**, on StressPresso's
meaning questions from 69 to **89**, and on choosing the meaning a stressed word implies (DEBATE, held-out) from 85 to **93**, with the
other decisions about the same.
**v1.4** understands far more languages: **Japanese** error goes from 33 % to **12 %** (FLEURS) and from 38 % to
**11 %** on conversational Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese error falls to a quarter to a third of v1.3, Thai,
Arabic and Russian error by 30–40 %, and Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (laughter, breath, drawl, stutter …) are much sharper.
**v1.5** hears the **whole clip**: earlier versions (like every Qwen3-ASR-based checkpoint we trained) dropped the
last ~4 % of every 30 s audio chunk, because the connector assumed 6.25 audio tokens per second while the encoder
emits 6.5. v1.5 is retrained on the true length, which sharpens the decisions that depend on the end of an utterance:
**end-of-turn** (Smart Turn test set 93.3 → **94.4**, Chinese 91.4 → **94.6**; LiveKit eot-bench English false
cut-offs at 300 ms 20.4 → **17.7 %**), **stress** (StressTest 81.7 → **85.3**), and **emotion** in natural speech
(LISTEN emotion 32.4 → **33.2**, LISTEN non-verbal 48.8 → **51.6**), with spoken QA up a point as well.

> **v1.5 (2026-11-03)** replaces v1.4 (2026-10-22): audio is read at its true length (`"audio_full_length": true`
> in `config.json`). **Use `duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` / `duplexjev>=0.7`**, which read this flag; older versions still
> load the model but cut the last ~4 % of each 30 s chunk, as before.
> Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.4`, `v1.3`, `v1.2`, `v1.1` and `v1.0` (`--revision v1.4` in vLLM,
> `revision="v1.4"` in `from_pretrained`).

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + the language model of Qwen3-VL-32B, 33.0 B parameters, bf16; one 80 GB GPU).

**Which 32B to pick.** This one, for everything above.

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-32B-Turn we trained the connector and a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here) for 4,000
steps. The mix is the 32B-Turn mix plus:

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| stress / pause detection (as in 32B-Stress: DEBATE, Stress-17K, TinyStress-15K, Expresso, neutral negatives) | which word is stressed, or none; where the pause is |
| speaker pairs (VoxCeleb1 dev, AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech, two-speaker mixtures) | same speaker or not; is this person in the clip |
| non-verbal sounds (VocalSound, NonVerbalSpeech-38K, NonverbalTTS, Expresso laughing) | is there laughter / breathing / a cough / a sigh / sniffing / throat clearing / a sneeze / crying …; negatives are cut from the same recordings away from the event |
| speaking style (EARS, Expresso whisper) | whispering, loud, fast, slow, high or low pitch, normal |
| spoken multiple-choice replay (ARC, OpenBookQA and CommonsenseQA train splits read by TTS) | keeps "answer the content" from being crowded out by "listen to the voice" |
| **v1.1:** conversation replay (spoken and typed user turns, up to 6 earlier turns as history; target = the original LLM's own reply) and in-house chat items | normal, full-length replies; trained with per-row loss averaging so long replies do not swamp the one-token decisions |
| **v1.2:** accents (VCTK, English Dialects, EdAcc, Common Voice accent labels, KeSpeech; held-out speakers kept for testing) | which accent: 19 English accents and 9 Mandarin dialect regions; native speaker or not; standard Mandarin or not; which English region |
| **v1.2:** end of turn right after a pause (otoSpeech-141h cut 0.2 s into each pause, with DualTurn labels; Smart Turn v3.2 training set) | finished vs. still talking / hesitating when the user has just gone quiet, the way a live voice agent has to decide |
| **v1.3:** the stress data re-balanced (more "which meaning does this stress imply" items, weight raised) and the gender data weighted ×2; no new corpora | choosing the meaning a stressed word implies; keeping gender where it was |
| **v1.4:** weak-language speech (ja, ko, vi, th, ar, ru: Emilia, Emilia-YODAS, YODAS2, Zeroth-Korean, VIVOS, FLEURS train, Common Voice; 162 k, labels re-checked with Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) + continuation (36 k) | transcribe and understand these languages |
| **v1.4:** Japanese speech (Emilia JA, Emilia-YODAS JA, Common Voice ja and other Japanese speech data; 358 k, re-checked) + Japanese continuation (20 k) | Japanese close to Chinese and English |
| **v1.4:** Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only; 42 k questions) | laughter, laughing while talking, breath, lip smack, sniff, cough, stressed word, drawl, which character is drawn out, stutter, sudden noise, unnatural pause, sentence emotion |
| **v1.4:** more emotion classes (surprise, fear, anxiety, excitement, encouragement, apologetic, playful) from CSEMOTIONS, EmotionTalk, DailyTalk, JL-Corpus, EMNS, Emozionalmente, SUBESCO | emotions beyond the basic four |
| **v1.5:** the whole v1.4 mix again, now with audio tokens at the encoder's true length (6.5 per second); transcription items with native-language instructions and leading / trailing silence (FLEURS dev split, the v1.4 weak-language speech); a light replay of all emotion data | the end of every clip is heard; always transcribe when asked to; emotion kept sharp |

v1.4 was trained from v1.3 in four short stages (2,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 1,000 steps; connector + a new rank-16 LoRA
each time, merged here), replaying the full v1.3 mix in every stage; the last two stages raise the stress,
non-verbal, emotion and speaking-style replay ×1.5 each.

v1.5 was trained from v1.4 in two stages (2,000 + 1,500 steps; connector + a new rank-16 LoRA each time, merged
here) with the audio-token count computed from the encoder's real output length.

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" "duplexjev-vllm>=0.4"
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para --max-model-len 4096
```

`duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` reads `"audio_full_length": true` from `config.json` and feeds the whole clip; `DJ_FULL_LEN=0`
forces the old truncated length, `DJ_FULL_LEN=1` the full length for any checkpoint.

Prompt format and client are the same as for [DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn);
see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Examples:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Is there laughter in this audio?

Options:
A. Yes
B. No

Answer with the letter only.
```

```
用户说：<|audio|>

除了说话，这段音频里还有哪种声音？

选项：
A. 叹气
B. 咳嗽
C. 笑声
D. 都没有

请只回答选项字母。
```

Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions; the model was trained with it.

## Limitations

- Accent and same-speaker scores were not re-measured for v1.4 / v1.5.
- Thai and Arabic are still 2–3× the encoder's own error.
- Non-verbal training audio is mostly acted (radio drama, animation, studio recordings); in natural conversation the
  scores are lower (see the table).
- Breathing in natural Mandarin conversation is weak (AUC 0.56 in v1.2, 0.65 in v1.1, 0.78 in v1.0); acted / read
  speech is much better.
- Accent answers describe how someone sounds, not where they are from or who they are; accents are often mixed or
  ambiguous. Do not use them to make decisions about people.
- Asked about itself, it may describe abilities (seeing images, speaking) that this checkpoint does not have on its
  own: it takes speech and text and replies in text.
- Speaker judgments are coarse (EER 18–40%) and must not be used to identify or verify people.
- Emotion labels come from acted corpora; do not use the outputs to make decisions about individuals.

# Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602: transcribe.cpp GGUF

GGUF conversions of [mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602) for use
with [transcribe.cpp](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp).

Ported from upstream commit
[2769294](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602/commit/2769294),
pinned 2026-06-06.
Validated against the Transformers reference at transcribe.cpp commit
[483c122](https://github.com/handy-computer/transcribe.cpp/tree/483c122)
on 2026-06-06.

Streaming audio-LLM speech-to-text. A ~970M causal audio encoder (left-pad
causal conv stem + 32-layer sliding-window RoPE transformer) feeds a
4-frame-group projector whose audio embeddings are added onto a ~3.4B
Ministral decoder (26 layers, GQA 32/8, NEOX RoPE) with delay-token latency
conditioning, emitting one text token per 80 ms audio slot (12.5 Hz). Takes a
16 kHz mono WAV and supports both incremental streaming (configurable
latency/quality via --stream-chunk-ms and --stream-voxtral-delay) and offline
transcription using an accuracy-first 2400 ms delay. Architecturally distinct
from the offline Voxtral 2507 family — own arch, streaming frontend, causal
encoder, additive audio fusion.

# Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime 2602

Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime 2602 is a **multilingual, realtime speech-transcription model** and among the first open-source solutions to achieve accuracy comparable to offline systems with a delay of **<500ms**.
It supports **13 languages** and outperforms existing open-source baselines across a range of tasks, making it ideal for applications like voice assistants and live subtitling.

Built with a **natively streaming architecture** and a custom causal audio encoder - it allows configurable transcription delays (240ms to 2.4s), enabling users to balance **latency and accuracy** based on their needs. 
At a **480ms delay**, it matches the performance of leading offline open-source transcription models, as well as realtime APIs.

As a **4B-parameter model**, is optimized for **on-device deployment**, requiring minimal hardware resources. 
It runs in realtime with on devices minimal hardware with throughput exceeding 12.5 tokens/second.

This model is released in **BF16** under the **Apache-2 license**, ensuring flexibility for both research and commercial use.

For more details, see our:
- [Blog post](https://mistral.ai/news/voxtral-transcribe-2)
- [Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-Realtime)
- [Technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11298)
- [vLLM's blog on streaming input](https://blog.vllm.ai/2026/01/31/streaming-realtime.html)


## Key Features
Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime consists of two main architectural components:
- **≈3.4B Language Model**
- **≈970M Audio Encoder**
- The audio encoder was trained from scratch with causal attention enabling streaming capability
- Both the audio encoder as well as the LLM backbone use sliding window attention allowing for "infinite" streaming
- For more details, refer to the [technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11298)

![Voxtral-Realtime Architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sanchit-gandhi/notebooks/refs/heads/main/voxtral-realtime.jpeg)

The Voxtral Mini 4B Realtime model offers the following capabilities:
- **High-Quality Transcription**: Transcribe audio to text with confidence.
- **Multilingual**: Supports dozens of languages, making it perfect for multilingual transcription tasks.
- **Real-Time**: Fast streaming ASR model, enabling real-time transcription use cases.
- **Configurable Transcription Delays**: Customize the transcription delay to balance quality and latency, from 80ms to 2.4s.

### Use Cases
**Real-Time Transcription Purposes:**
- Private meeting transcriptions
- Live subtitle creation
- Real-time assistants with speech understanding
- And more

Bringing real-time transcription capabilities to all.

### Recommended Settings

We recommend deploying with the following best practices:
- Always set the temperature to 0.0
- A single text-token is worth 80ms. Hence, make sure to set your `--max-model-len` accordingly. To live-record a 1h meeting, you need to set `--max-model-len >= 3600 / 0.8 = 45000`.
  In theory, you should be able to record with no limit; in practice, pre-allocations of RoPE parameters among other things limits `--max-model-len`.
  For the best user experience, we recommend to simply instantiate vLLM with the default parameters which will automatically set a maximum model length of 131072 (~ca. 3h).
- We strongly recommend using websockets to set up audio streaming sessions. For more info on how to do so, check [Usage](#usage).
- We recommend using a delay of 480ms as we found it to be the sweet spot of performance and low latency. If, however, you want to adapt the delay, you can change the `"transcription_delay_ms": 480` parameter
  in the [tekken.json](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602/blob/main/tekken.json) file to any multiple of 80ms between 80 and 1200, as well as 2400 as a standalone value.

```
uv pip install -U vllm
```

Doing so should automatically install [`mistral_common >= 1.9.0`](https://github.com/mistralai/mistral-common/releases/tag/v1.9.0).

To check:
```
python -c "import mistral_common; print(mistral_common.__version__)"
```

You can also make use of a ready-to-go [docker image](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile) or on the [docker hub](https://hub.docker.com/layers/vllm/vllm-openai/nightly/images/sha256-6ae33f5001ab9d32346ce2c82c660fe57021c4f0c162ed0c60b843319829b810).

Make sure to also install all required audio processing libraries:

```
uv pip install soxr librosa soundfile
```

Also we recommend using Transformers v5 as v4 can clutter the terminal with unnecessary warnings (see [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34642))

```
uv pip install --upgrade transformers
```

#### Serve

Due to size and the BF16 format of the weights - `Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602` can run on a single GPU with >= 16GB memory.

The model can be launched in both "eager" mode:

```bash
VLLM_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1 vllm serve mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602 --compilation_config '{"cudagraph_mode": "PIECEWISE"}'
```

Additional flags:
* You can set `--max-num-batched-tokens` to balance throughput and latency, higher means higher throughput but higher latency.
* You can reduce the default `--max-model-len` to allocate less memory for the pre-computed RoPE frequencies,
  if you are certain that you won't have to transcribe for more than X hours. By default the model uses a `--max-model-len` of 131072 (> 3h).

### Transformers

Starting with `transformers >= 5.2.0`, you can run Voxtral Realtime natively in Transformers!

For more details, refer to the [Transformers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/voxtral_realtime).

#### Installation

Install Transformers:

```bash
pip install --upgrade transformers
```

Make sure to have `mistral-common` installed with audio dependencies:

```bash
pip install --upgrade "mistral-common[audio]"
```

#### Usage

```python
from transformers import VoxtralRealtimeForConditionalGeneration, AutoProcessor
from mistral_common.tokens.tokenizers.audio import Audio
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

repo_id = "mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime-2602"

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(repo_id)
model = VoxtralRealtimeForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(repo_id, device_map="auto")

repo_id = "patrickvonplaten/audio_samples"
audio_file = hf_hub_download(repo_id=repo_id, filename="bcn_weather.mp3", repo_type="dataset")

audio = Audio.from_file(audio_file, strict=False)
audio.resample(processor.feature_extractor.sampling_rate)

inputs = processor(audio.audio_array, return_tensors="pt")
inputs = inputs.to(model.device, dtype=model.dtype)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs)
decoded_outputs = processor.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)

print(decoded_outputs[0])
```
